question: Therapeutic massage offers proven benefits for physical and mental health. The gentle pressure and rhythmic movements stimulate blood circulation, enhancing tissue oxygenation and reducing muscle tension, while contributing to the regulation of blood pressure and heart rate through activation of the parasympathetic nervous system.

On a psychological level, they reduce cortisol and increase serotonin and endorphins, improving sleep and a sense of wellbeing. At the same time, this practice has proven beneficial for reducing chronic pain, anxiety and fatigue, as well as for restoring mobility in musculoskeletal diseases.

The involvement of kinesiotherapists and physiotherapists is crucial for the correct and safe application of these techniques, ensuring scientifically documented preventive and rehabilitative interventions. In addition to its therapeutic value, massage can act as a means of early detection of inflammation, stiffness or circulatory problems, promoting timely medical assessment.

Given that this is a low-cost and non-invasive practice, with potentially significant benefits for public health: Could the Commission, within the framework of the open method of coordination in the health sector, encourage Member States to adopt common guidelines for the coverage of a limited number of therapeutic massage and physiotherapy sessions per year by national health systems, as a preventive measure and to promote well-being?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.1.2026) According to Article 168 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Member States are responsible for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care, including the reimbursement of treatments1. Therefore, it is up to Member States to decide on the coverage of treatments by national health systems.

As announced in the President of the Commission’s Political Guidelines2 and the mission letter for the Commissioner on Health and Animal Welfare3, the Commission will step up its work on preventive health. Under the ‘Healthier Together’ initiative4, the Commission supports Member States in developing and implementing actions on health promotion and prevention of non-communicable diseases.

Examples include the joint actions PreventNCD5 that addresses health determinants and MENTOR6 that promotes mental health and wellbeing. In addition, the Commission supports the collection and sharing of proven practices via the EU Best Practice Portal on Public Health7.

The Commission regularly exchanges views with Member States via the Expert Group on Public Health8 on how to address public health challenges, and to promote coordination of initiatives based on national and EU priorities.
1 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/treaty/tfeu_2008/art_168/oj/eng. 2 Political Guidelines for the next European Commission 2024-2029.
